whyItMatters: The single story that reorders your Sunday is the BC election: Conservatives have swept to a majority, David Eby has resigned, and Lorne Doerkson becomes premier-elect. For you that is not spectator news — you own property in Sun Peaks, Langley and Vancouver, and a new government campaigning on investment, tax cuts and "getting BC back on track" will touch short-term-rental rules, housing supply policy, and the public-sector climate your higher-ed clients operate inside. Watch the next ninety days for signals on whether the NDP's STR registry and speculation measures survive, soften, or get rebuilt. Locally, Peter Milobar holds Kamloops, which keeps your region inside the governing caucus — useful context for anything municipal. Beyond politics, there's a genuinely historic science story — the first effective cancer vaccine clearing trials — and a thin but real higher-ed thread on tuition pressure. There's no meaningful AI or martech news in today's cycle, so this is a day to read the political tea leaves, not the technology ones.
audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Sunday, October twenty-fifth, twenty twenty-six, and the ground shifted in British Columbia overnight — so that's where we start.

The headline you need before anything else: British Columbia has a new government. The Conservatives have swept to a majority — a genuine landslide — and David Eby's NDP has collapsed. Eby himself has resigned as party leader, apologizing to the MLAs who lost their seats in the party's unravelling. Lorne Doerkson, the Cariboo MLA who led the Conservatives as interim leader, will be premier-elect. This is the update to the story I flagged on Friday, when I told you the vote was happening and Eby's job was on the line. It was — and he lost it. For a province that has been under NDP governance for the better part of a decade, this is as close to a political earthquake as BC gets, and it happened on lower voter turnout, which the analysts are already picking apart.

Now, why does this land in your real estate section rather than filed away as general politics? Because you own property in three BC markets — Sun Peaks, Langley, and Vancouver — and because real estate is a live lane in your practice. A change of government at the provincial level is the single biggest lever on the rules that govern what you can do with those properties. Think about what the NDP built over the last several years: the short-term-rental registry and the principal-residence restrictions, the speculation and vacancy tax, the flipping tax, aggressive housing-supply mandates on municipalities. All of that is now in the hands of a party that campaigned on cutting taxes, attracting investment, and — in Doerkson's own words on election night — getting BC "back on track" and appealing to businesses and young people to stay in the province.

That's the second story worth your attention: the catalogue of what the incoming Conservatives actually promised. Lower taxes, expanded natural gas production, investment attraction, public safety, healthcare. What's conspicuously unresolved in that platform is the fate of the short-term-rental framework. A pro-investment, pro-property-owner government has every ideological reason to loosen the STR rules the NDP tightened — but they also inherit a housing affordability crisis that those rules were meant to address, and unwinding them is politically fraught. So I would not assume quick repeal. I'd watch the first ninety days for signals: cabinet appointments, throne-speech language, and whether they touch the registry, the principal-residence rule, or the speculation tax. For your Sun Peaks and Langley holdings specifically, any softening of STR enforcement is a direct operational variable. This is worth a short, measured content piece from you — not a hot take on the politics, but a clear-eyed read on what a change of government means for the public-sector and institutional environment: how policy direction, data governance, and FIPPA priorities can shift when the party in power changes. That's your public-institution governance lens applied to a live BC event, and almost nobody in your lane will write it with that framing.

One more real estate note that sits underneath all of this: there's a looming Bank of Canada decision, and a Globe column over the weekend framed it as a genuine dilemma — do you raise rates to battle inflation, or hold to protect an economy strained by the trade war. Either way, the rate backdrop is the quiet governor of buyer activity and mortgage costs heading into year-end. For your husband's brokerage and for the real estate lane of your practice, that's the number that matters more than any single listing trend. Keep it in the corner of your eye.

Closer to home, the election result has a Kamloops chapter. Peter Milobar has been re-elected, returning for a fourth term as the Kamloops MLA, alongside Ward Stamer in the neighbouring riding — both Conservatives, both now part of the governing caucus for the first time in nearly a century of this party's existence. What that means practically is that your region is no longer represented by opposition members shut out of power; it's inside the tent. For anything municipal — Kamloops council business, Thompson Rivers University funding, regional infrastructure like the RIH questions that have been swirling — having your MLAs in government rather than opposition changes the dynamics of who gets heard. It's a quiet but real shift in the local power map, and worth filing.

And because the weekend wasn't entirely politics: a Kamloops designer has landed a spot on Project Runway Canada, described as a once-in-a-lifetime experience. A nice bit of local colour and a reminder that the talent pipeline out of a city that size is deeper than outsiders assume. Small story, but it's the kind of community texture that makes a place feel like home.

Onto higher education, where the cycle is thin but there's a thread worth pulling. Students in Prince Edward Island are facing tuition hikes more than double the national average. On its own, PEI is a small market — but treat it as a canary. The mechanism behind these increases is the revenue squeeze that smaller Canadian institutions are now living through, as the international-student caps and the broader federal restrictions choke off the overseas tuition that was quietly subsidizing domestic operations. When the foreign-student revenue drops, the money has to come from somewhere, and increasingly it comes from domestic tuition, program cuts, or deficits. This is the structural story underneath so much of the higher-ed news I've been bringing you — the MUN enrolment drop, the UK's falling visa numbers, the Australian migration politics. The institutions you sell into are all doing this math right now, and the ones who survive well will be the ones who get sharper about recruitment efficiency and brand differentiation rather than just raising prices. That's your opening.

And an update on a story I covered Friday: the McGill law-school controversy. The paroled convicted murderer whose presence in the faculty of law sparked duelling student petitions has now been returned to custody. That defuses, at least for now, an acute reputational flashpoint for McGill — but it's a reminder of how fast a single admissions-and-conduct situation can become a brand crisis for an institution. The crisis-comms lesson there is one your higher-ed clients should internalize: the governance failure isn't always the decision itself, it's the absence of a clear framework for making and explaining it.

Now a story that's genuinely historic, and I want to give it its due. STAT News reports that after roughly a hundred years of trying, there is finally an effective cancer vaccine. This is the Merck and Moderna mRNA candidate — intismeran — which has cleared its trials, and the race is now on to extend it beyond its first success into more tumour types. Let me be precise about what this is and isn't. It's not a preventive shot you get at the pharmacy; it's a therapeutic vaccine, trained to teach a patient's immune system to recognize and attack their specific tumour. The first win came in melanoma, building on the kind of immunotherapy combinations we've seen reshape that disease over the past few years. What makes this a landmark is the platform: if mRNA vaccines can be personalized to a tumour's mutations and shown to work, the same machinery that gave us the COVID vaccines becomes a template for oncology broadly. For you and your family, the near-term takeaway is simply awareness — this is the direction cancer treatment is moving, and the next few years of trials in lung, pancreatic, and other cancers are the ones to watch. It's rare that I get to bring you a health story that's unambiguously good news from a source as rigorous as STAT. This is one of them.

On the broader stage, a few things belong on your radar. First, an update on the national story I previewed: First Nations leaders are gathering with Prime Minister Carney and the premiers in Ottawa today for a day of ceremony ahead of a historic meeting on national priorities. This matters for the tone of federal-Indigenous-provincial relations going forward, and it's happening in the same news cycle as BC electing a new government — so the premiers' table itself is about to look different.

Second, Serbia held a parliamentary election cast as a showdown between the populist leader Aleksandar Vucic and a sustained student-led protest movement. I flag it not because Serbia drives your week, but because it's a clean case study in whether entrenched leaders can outlast organized youth mobilization — a pattern playing out in several democracies right now, and one worth understanding as a senior leader reading the global mood.

And third, a data point from the UK budget: the British government is earmarking one billion pounds for social and affordable housing, pushing that ten-year programme past forty billion. I mention it as a comparative signal — major economies across the board are leaning on public spending to attack housing supply shortfalls, the same problem BC's new government now has to solve from the other ideological direction. The contrast between the UK's public-build approach and a BC Conservative investment-and-deregulation approach is, frankly, a useful frame for anyone thinking seriously about housing policy.

Finally, one BC safety item for your awareness. In North Vancouver, RCMP rescued one hundred and fifty young people and their chaperones after the cruise vessel they were on ran aground on a sandbar. By the reports, everyone was brought to safety. It's the kind of local incident that's more unsettling than tragic — a graduation cruise gone sideways — but with family in BC, these are exactly the small-scale events I'll keep surfacing so you're never caught off guard by something close to home.

So here's where I'd point your attention this week, Midya. The BC election is the story that keeps giving — the policy consequences will unspool over months, and you are positioned to read them through a lens almost no one else in your field has: property owner, real estate advisor, and public-institution governance specialist all at once. Watch the first moves of the Doerkson government on short-term rentals and public-sector priorities, and consider getting a thoughtful piece out early, before the consensus forms. There's no AI or martech news worth your time today, and that's fine — not every Sunday is a technology day. Rest a little, let the political dust settle, and we'll reconvene tomorrow when the new cabinet picture starts to sharpen. Talk soon.
